en: The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in the city of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove.
At the Anāthapiṇḍika Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having finished his almsround through the city in sequence, he returned to his original location.

When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and as usual spread out his seat. He sat down cross-legged, holding his body erect and dwelling in unmoving right mindfulness.
At that time, the bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

Then, the venerable Subhūti, from among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, stood respectfully, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “It is rare!
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva, within the Great Vehicle, resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
How should they dwell?
How should they practice?
"How does one subdue the mind?
At that time, the Buddha told Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent!
Subhūti! It is as you have said:
"The Tathāgata well protects and attends to all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas."
"Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
As for a Bodhisattva in the Mahāyāna who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should abide in this way, practice in this way, and subdue their mind in this way."
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, it is so.”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"All bodhisattvas give rise to such a thought:"

"Of all sentient beings, those comprised within the realm of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all sentient beings included within the realm of sentient beings, I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation."
"In this way, although he brings immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Why is this, Subhūti?"
If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a sentient being, they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
"If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, they are not called a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on things; they practice giving without dwelling anywhere. They do not dwell on form when practicing giving, nor do they dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving."
Subhūti! A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, not dwelling upon the perception of signs. Why is that?
"If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, the mass of their merit cannot be measured or conceived.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can the space of the eastern direction be measured?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"So it is, Subhūti! Can the emptiness of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured?"
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! For a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling on signs, the mass of merit is likewise immeasurable and inconceivable."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:
“A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner alone. “Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the accomplishment of marks? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
One cannot see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of physical marks. Why is this? [Because...]"
"The characteristics described by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not characteristics.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Whatever characteristics exist are all false speech."
"If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one does not speak falsely.
To see thus that all marks are non-marks is to see the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Will there be any sentient beings in the future age, in the final period, who, upon hearing such chapters and verses of this sutra, will give rise to the perception of reality?”
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "Do not speak thus:
'Will there be any sentient beings in the future age, in the final period, who, upon hearing such chapters and verses of this sūtra, will give rise to the perception of reality?'"
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

"In a future age, at the end of time, when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who observe the precepts and cultivate merit and wisdom; they will be able to give rise to faith in the chapters and verses of this sūtra and regard them as true."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

"You should know that those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have not practiced and made offerings under only one, two, three, four, or five buddhas; nor have they planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five buddhas."
The Buddha again addressed Subhūti:

"They have practiced and made offerings under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Buddhas, and have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Buddhas."
"Subhūti, if anyone hears this sūtra and is able to give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment,
the Tathāgata fully knows all such sentient beings; the Tathāgata fully sees all such sentient beings."
Subhūti! These bodhisattvas produce such an immeasurable mass of merit and take up such immeasurable merit. Why is this?
Subhūti! These bodhisattvas no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span. Subhūti!
These bodhisattvas have no perception of dharmas, nor do they have a perception of the non-existence of dharmas.
They have no perception, nor do they have a perception of non-perception. Why is this?
Subhūti! If these bodhisattvas were to grasp at the marks of dharmas, they would then be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva has the notion of dharmas, they are attached to the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a life-span.
Why is this? Subhūti!
One should not grasp at dharmas, nor should one fail to grasp them.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has always spoken of the dharma-gate of the raft parable: these dharmas should be relinquished, yet it is not for the sake of relinquishing dharmas that they are relinquished.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the venerable Subhūti: “Subhūti,
what do you think?”
“Does the Tathāgata attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Does the Tathāgata have any dharma that he teaches? Subhūti replied:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can teach."
Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are neither graspable nor expressible; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. Why is this?
"All noble ones are named after the dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Subhūti,
what do you think?"
Suppose one were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift.
Subhūti, what do you think?
“Would the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family be great?
Subhūti replied, “It would be very great, Bhagavān!”
"Very much, Sugata! Those sons and daughters of good family will gain very great merit. Why is that?"
“World-Honored One!
This accumulation of merit is itself not an accumulation of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of an ‘accumulation of merit, an accumulation of merit.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift;”

If, moreover, one were to receive, uphold, and even explain as little as a four-line verse from this sutra to others, their merit would surpass that of the former by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.
Why is this? Subhūti!
All the dharmas of the unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas issue forth from this sutra.
All Buddhas, Tathāgatas, are born from this sūtra.
Subhūti, what are called "Buddha-dharmas," Buddha-dharmas, are not, in fact, Buddha-dharmas.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna ever have such a thought as this:”
"Did you think, 'I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
Truly, there is no dharma named 'srotāpanna'."
"Not entering into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena— this is called a srotāpanna. The Buddha said, "Subhūti!"
What do you think?
Does a once-returner have this thought:
‘I have attained the fruit of a once-returner’?
"No, World-Honored One," Subhūti replied.
Why is this? Because, in reality, there is no dharma named "once-returner.
It is merely designated as "once-returner."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can an Anāgāmin form such a thought as this:”
"Did you think, 'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'? Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
Because, in reality, there is no dharma that can be called 'Anāgāmin'."
"This is called an Anāgāmin. "Subhūti, what do you think?"
Can an Arhat have this thought: "I have attained Arhatship"? No.
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
"In truth, there is no dharma called 'Arhat,' World-Honored One!
If an Arhat were to have such a thought:"
"If I were to think, 'I have attained arhatship,' I would immediately be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life span.
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha has declared that I am foremost among those who have attained the samādhi of non-contention; the World-Honored One has declared that I am an arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One!
I do not harbor such thoughts:
"I am an Arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One!
If I were to have such a thought:
"I have attained arhatship," yet the World-Honored One did not designate me as foremost among those who practice the way of non-contention (*araṇā*).
This is because Subhūti has, in reality, nothing at all that he practices; it is for this reason that Subhūti is named "the one of non-contention" and "one who practices non-contention."
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?
When the Tathāgata was formerly with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did he obtain any dharma of anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One!
While the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he did not, in reality, obtain any *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* regarding the Dharma.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If a bodhisattva were to say: 'I adorn the buddha-fields,' [he would be speaking falsely]."
"That Bodhisattva speaks untruthfully. Why is this? Subhūti!"
That which the Tathāgata has described as the adornment of Buddha-fields is in fact no adornment; it is merely called the adornment of Buddha-fields.

Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: without abiding anywhere; not giving rise to the mind by abiding in forms, nor giving rise to the mind by abiding in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; they should give rise to that mind without abiding anywhere.
“Subhūti! It is as if there were a person whose body were like Sumeru, the king of mountains. Subhūti!”
"What do you think? Is this body great? Subhūti replied:
"Extremely great, World-Honored One!
Why is this? The Buddha has taught that what is not a body is called the 'Great Body'."
"That body is not a body; it is called the 'Great Body.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; what do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous?"
Subhūti said: "Very many, World-Honored One!
Even the Ganges Rivers alone are already innumerable, let alone their sands."
The Buddha said,
“Subhūti! I now speak these words to you in truth.”
If there were good sons or good daughters who, with the seven treasures, filled as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and offered them as gifts to all the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas— Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Would those sons or daughters of good family acquire much merit? Subhūti replied:
“Very much, World-Honored One!
Those sons and daughters of good family would obtain very great merit.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If one were to fill as many worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift;

yet if a son or daughter of good family, from this Dharma-door, were to even receive and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it to others, this merit would surpass the former merit by immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya*."

"Furthermore, Subhūti! Wherever this Dharma-gate is taught, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha."
How much more so for anyone who is able to fully receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra! Subhūti,
you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare dharma.
"Wherever this sutra may be located, there is a Buddha, or one who is as venerable as a Buddha.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should this Dharma-door be named?
How should we uphold it? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"This Dharma-gate is named 'The Perfection of Wisdom, Like a Diamond.
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is that?
Subhūti! What the Buddha calls the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) is not, in fact, a perfection of wisdom. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has not preached any Dharma. “Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Are all the atoms contained within a trichiliocosm many? Subhūti replied:
“There are very many atoms of dust,
World-Honored One. “Subhūti!
These atoms, the Tathāgata says, are not atoms; they are called "atoms.
The world-system, the Tathāgata says, is not a world-system; it is called a "world-system."
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"Why is this? What the Tathāgata has preached as the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are in fact no marks; they are merely named the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, for as many lifetimes as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, gave away their bodies and lives in charity; yet if there were another person who, from within this Dharma-door, were to receive, uphold, or even recite as little as a four-line verse and explain it to others, the merit of the latter would be far greater—immeasurable and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya).”

At that time, when Subhūti heard this sutra being preached, he deeply understood its meaning and intent; weeping with tears of sorrow, he wiped away his tears and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, Bhagavān!"
"How rare, Sugata! That the Buddha has preached such a profound Dharma-gate; from the past until now, with the eye of wisdom I have attained, I have never before heard such a Dharma-gate."
"Why is this? Subhūti! What the Buddha calls 'prajñāpāramitā' is not, in fact, prajñāpāramitā."
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who hear this sutra and their faith becomes pure, they will give rise to the mark of reality; you should know that such persons are said to have accomplished the foremost and most rare merit.”
World-Honored One!
This true mark is itself no mark.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "true mark," the "true mark."
“World-Honored One!
That I should now hear such a Dharma-gate and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.
But if, in a future age, there should be sentient beings who hear this Dharma-gate and believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, those people would be the most rare and extraordinary of all.”
Why is this? Because this person has no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a sentient being, and no notion of a life-span. Why is this?
The mark of a self is itself no-mark;
the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks. Why is this?
"To be free from all marks is what is called 'the Buddhas.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is!"
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear it, you should know that such a person is most rare.
Why is this? Subhūti!
The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost pāramitā, yet it is not a foremost pāramitā.
That which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is also called a pāramitā by immeasurable Buddhas; therefore, it is named the foremost pāramitā.
“Subhūti! What the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is not, in fact, a perfection of patience. Why is this?

Subhūti! When in the past I was having my body cut limb from limb by King Kaliṅga, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a sentient being, no perception of a person, and no perception of a life-span; there was neither form, nor was there the absence of form.
Why is this? Subhūti,

if at the time in the past when my body was being dismembered limb by limb, I had possessed the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.

Subhūti! Furthermore, I recall that in the past, during five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi of patience; throughout those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a sentient being, no mark of a person, and no mark of a life-span.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should depart from all marks and resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?
If the mind has a dwelling place, it is not truly dwelling.

One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
Therefore the Buddha said:
"The Bodhisattva’s mind does not dwell on form when practicing giving. Subhūti!
“A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner. Subhūti said,
“World-Honored One!”
The marks of all sentient beings are, in fact, no-marks. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said:
"All sentient beings are, in truth, not sentient beings. "Subhūti,
the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, and speaks that which is not otherwise."
Subhūti! The Dharma attained by the Tathāgata and the Dharma taught by him are neither real nor false. Subhūti!
Subhūti, it is just as if a person were to enter the darkness and see nothing at all;
so too it is with a bodhisattva whose mind dwells on phenomena while practicing generosity. Subhūti!
For example, it is as if a person with eyes, when the night has ended and the light of the sun shines forth, sees various forms and colors.
If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on things, it is also like this.
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

If there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this Dharma-gate, then the Tathāgata, by means of the Buddha’s wisdom, fully knows these people, fully sees these people, and fully awakens to these people; they shall all achieve an immeasurable and boundless accumulation of merit."

“Subhūti! If there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; during the middle part of the day, again gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and during the latter part of the day, again gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—thus relinquishing immeasurable bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas by means of such bodily giving.

If there should be another person who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, believes with faith and does not slander it, their merit would be immeasurably and incalculably greater than that; how much more so for one who copies, receives, upholds, reads, recites, practices it, and explains it extensively for others.
“Subhūti! To speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
This Dharma-gate was taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.”

If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, and explain it extensively for others, the Tathāgata knows these people and sees these people; they all achieve an inconceivable, ineffable, boundless, and immeasurable mass of merit.
Such persons as these, Subhūti, shall indeed bear the burden of the Tathāgata’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Why is this? Subhūti!
If one delights in inferior teachings, they will be unable to receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this sutra for others.
It is impossible that anyone who holds views of a self, a sentient being, a person, or a life-span could receive, uphold, read, recite, practice, or explain this Dharma-gate for others.
“Subhūti! Wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the world—gods, humans, and asuras.”

"You should know that this place shall be treated as a stūpa; it should be honored by all, who should pay homage, circumambulate it, and scatter various flowers and incense upon that spot. Furthermore, Subhūti!"
If good sons or good daughters receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they will be treated with contempt by others. Why is this?

Because the karmic offenses of these persons from previous lives, which would have caused them to fall into the evil realms, are extinguished by the contempt shown by people in the present life; they shall thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Subhūti! I recall that in the past, during immeasurable, incalculable, incalculable kalpas before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eighty-four billion nayutas of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas. I personally attended upon and made offerings to them all; none were passed by in vain.”
Subhūti! Such immeasurable Buddhas as these, I have all personally served and made offerings to, none having been in vain.

If there should be another person who, in a future age at the end of time, is able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, the merit they obtain would be such that the merit from my offerings to all those Buddhas does not equal even one hundredth part of it; nor a thousandth, ten-thousandth, or a hundred-thousandth part; nor even a billionth part; nor can it be reached by any calculation or analogy.

“Subhūti! If there are good men or good women who, in a future age, at the end of time, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice this sutra, were I to fully describe the merit they would obtain, some who hear it might have their minds become deranged and confused, falling into doubt and lack of faith.”
“Subhūti! You should know that this Dharma-gate is inconceivable, and its karmic fruition is also inconceivable.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva resolve their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
How do they abide?”
"How should one practice?
How should one subdue the mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"A bodhisattva who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
'I shall bring all sentient beings to liberation, causing them to enter the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.'"
"Having thus brought all sentient beings to final nirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to final nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Subhūti!
"In reality, there is no dharma whatsoever that can be called 'a bodhisattva who has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma through which he attained anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Subhūti replied to the Buddha, “No, indeed!”
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi under Dīpaṃkara Buddha.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is! Subhūti!"
In truth, there is no dharma such that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Subhūti, if there were any dharma such that the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me the prediction [of my future enlightenment].
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Since there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, for this reason Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), speaking these words: "Māṇava!..."
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
That which is called "Tathāgata" is precisely true *tathatā*. "Subhūti!
If someone were to say:
“‘The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi’—
this person speaks what is not true, Subhūti!”
In truth, there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti,
regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, it is neither real nor false.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says:
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti!
Regarding what is called "all dharmas," all dharmas are indeed not all dharmas; therefore they are called "all dharmas.
"Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was magnificent and vast."
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrous greatness of the human body, it is not a great body; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘great body.’”
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, it is the same for a bodhisattva.”
If one says, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa," then that person is not a bodhisattva.
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, what do you think?”
“Is there any real dharma that is called a ‘bodhisattva’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"In reality, there is no dharma that can be called a 'bodhisattva.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
'In all dharmas, there is no sentient being, no person, and no life-spanner.'"
"Subhūti! If a bodhisattva should say:
'I adorn the buddha-fields.'"
Such a person is not called a bodhisattva. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the adornment of buddha-fields, that adornment of buddha-fields is actually no adornment; it is merely designated as the adornment of buddha-fields.
Subhūti! If a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of a self and the non-existence of phenomena, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva, a bodhisattva. Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?”
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.”
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
Subhūti replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye? Subhūti replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?”
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, what do you think?”
“Are all the grains of sand in the Ganges River what the Buddha calls ‘sand’? Subhūti replied,
“So it is, World-Honored One.”
“The Tathāgata says they are sand.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
"What do you think?

Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River; and suppose there were Buddha-worlds as numerous as all the grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers—would these worlds be many?"
Subhūti said: “That world-system is very numerous,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“In all those worlds, whatever sentient beings there are, and however many kinds of mental states they abide in, the Tathāgata knows them all.”
Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all abidings of the mind are, in fact, non-abidings of the mind; it is for this reason they are called "abidings of the mind. Why is this?
Subhūti! The past mind cannot be apprehended, the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended. "Subhūti!"
What do you think?
If someone were to take seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift, would that son or daughter of good family gain much merit by reason of this cause and condition?
Subhūti said: "So it is, World-Honored One!
By this cause and condition, that person would gain exceedingly great merit."
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
By this cause and condition, those sons of good family and daughters of good family will acquire a vast accumulation of merit.
Subhūti, if that accumulation of merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not speak of it as an "accumulation of merit, an accumulation of merit."
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his perfected physical body?”
Subhūti said: “No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the form-body.”
Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the "complete body of form" is not, in fact, a complete body of form; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "complete body of form."
The Buddha said: "Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One!”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of his possession of the various marks. Why is this?
What the Tathāgata calls the possession of all marks is itself a non-possession; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "possession of all marks."
The Buddha said: “Subhūti, what do you think?”
"Do you think that the Tathāgata has the thought: 'I shall preach some Dharma'?"
Subhūti! Do not have such a thought. Why is that?
If anyone says,
"The Tathāgata has preached a Dharma," they slander the Buddha, for they fail to understand what I have taught.
Why is this? Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of "speaking the Dharma," there is no dharma that can be spoken; it is merely called "speaking the Dharma."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith?”
The Buddha said:
“Subhūti! They are not sentient beings, nor are they non-sentient beings.”
Why is this? Subhūti, as for "sentient beings, sentient beings," the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; they are merely designated as "sentient beings."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, what do you think?”
“Does the Tathāgata attain anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi? Subhūti replied, “No!”
“World-Honored One!
World-Honored One, there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! In my Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is what is called 'Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi'."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal, without high or low; it is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Because there is no sentient being, no person, and no life-span, one attains the equality of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; all wholesome dharmas result in the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Subhūti! As for what are called ‘wholesome dharmas,’ the Tathāgata has said that they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as ‘wholesome dharmas. Subhūti!”

If someone were to take all the kings of mountains, the Sumerus, within a trichiliocosm, and offer such a heap of the seven precious jewels as a gift; and if another person were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even so much as a single four-line verse from this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the former merit would not equal a hundredth part of the latter, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor a kalā, nor a saṃkhyeya, nor an upaniṣad part; it would not even be reached by calculation, comparison, or analogy.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Do you suppose that the Tathāgata has such a thought as this:”
"Subhūti, do you think that [the Tathāgata thinks], 'I have delivered sentient beings'?"
Do not harbor such a thought. Why is this?
In reality, there is no sentient being whom the Tathāgata delivers.
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
If there were any real sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, the Tathāgata would possess the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.”
Subhūti! As the Tathāgata has said:
"That which is called 'having a self' is not actually a self; it is only the ignorant, ordinary worldlings who conceive of a self."
“Subhūti! Those who are born as ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*) are, according to the Tathāgata, said not to be born; therefore they are called ‘ordinary worldlings who are born. Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Can one see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of marks? Subhūti said:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught, one does not see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of physical marks.
The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is!”
"Subhūti! One does not see the Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of physical marks.
The Buddha said:

“Subhūti! If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of physical marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would be a Tathāgata. Therefore, it is not by the perfection of physical marks that the Tathāgata is seen.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me by means of sound,
Such a person follows a deviant path And cannot see the Tathāgata."
That wondrous body of the Tathāgata is precisely the Dharma-body of all Buddhas;
the essence of the Dharma cannot be seen, and that consciousness cannot know it. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Can a Tathāgata attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the accomplishment of the marks?
"Subhūti! [the Buddha said.]
Do not entertain this thought:
"The Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the perfection of physical marks. Subhūti!
Subhūti, if you should think:
"A bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* teaches the characteristic of the annihilation and cessation of all phenomena," [you would be mistaken]. Subhūti!
Do not conceive such a thought.
Why is this? A bodhisattva who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* does not speak of the characteristic of the annihilation or extinction of all phenomena.

“Subhūti! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take as many treasures of the seven jewels as would fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River and offer them as a gift;”
If there is a bodhisattva who knows that all dharmas are without self and attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas,
this merit surpasses the previously obtained merit. Subhūti!
“Because bodhisattvas do not grasp at merit.
Subhūti said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!”
“Does a bodhisattva not take hold of merit?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!...”
The Bodhisattva receives merit, yet does not grasp at merit; for this reason, the Bodhisattva takes up merit.
"Subhūti! If someone were to say:
"To say that 'the Tathāgata comes or goes, stands, sits, or lies down'—such a person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this? "
The Tathāgata has nowhere to go and nowhere from which he comes; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. "Subhūti!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to take the atoms of dust in a trichiliocosm..."
Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose those many worlds as numerous as atoms were ground into an asaṃkhyeya of atoms.
What do you think? How would you regard this?
"Would this multitude of atoms be considered many? Subhūti replied,
"That multitude of atoms would be very many."
World-Honored One!
Why is this? If these multitudes of subtle atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have spoken of them as "multitudes of subtle atoms."
Why is this? The Buddha speaks of a multitude of atoms, yet that is not a multitude of atoms; therefore, the Buddha speaks of a multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One!
The "trichiliocosm" spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a world; therefore, the Buddha speaks of the "trichiliocosm. Why is this?
If the world were truly existent, it would be a single, unified whole.
What the Tathāgata calls a "single, unified whole" is not actually a single, unified whole; therefore, the Buddha speaks of a "single, unified whole."
The Buddha said, “Subhūti!
That which is a unified mass is ineffable; it is only ordinary people who greedily cling to such things.”
Why is this? Subhūti! If someone were to speak thus:
"The Buddha has spoken of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being,
and the view of a life-span. Subhūti, what do you think?
"Is what this person says correct speech?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One!"
Why is this? World-Honored One!

When the Tathāgata speaks of the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, these are not actually views of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; they are merely designated as "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span."

“Subhūti! A bodhisattva who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and believe in them thus; in this way, they do not dwell upon the marks of phenomena.”

Why is this? Subhūti, as for what is called the "characteristic of dharmas," the Tathāgata says that this characteristic of dharmas is not a characteristic of dharmas; it is merely designated by the name "characteristic of dharmas."
Subhūti! If there were a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, were to offer them as a gift;

and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and, regarding this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it to others even if only as much as a four-line verse, their merit would surpass that of the former by immeasurable asaṃkhyeyas.
"How is it that one expounds for others without it being called 'expounding,' yet this is indeed called 'expounding'?
Then he spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena Are like stars, a visual impairment, a lamp, an illusion,"
"Like dew, a bubble, a dream, a flash of lightning, and a cloud—thus should one contemplate.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Regarding the *Vajracchedikā*, there have been six translations in total.
According to the *Kaiyuan Lu*, this is the second translation.

The *Sichuan* edition of the sutra has been lost to transmission; it erroneously re-translated the work of the Chen dynasty Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha and attributed it to the Wei dynasty Dharmaruci, which is a significant discrepancy.

Now, from among the treatises translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmaruci, we have extracted the original sūtra texts and carved them into printing blocks for circulation, hoping that those who read them will come to know their source.
Recorded on the day of the full moon in the first month of winter in the year of Xinsi of the Zhìyuán era, by the Nanshan Puning Sūtra Bureau.
